extracted.intended_audience: researchers, scientists, and institutional communicators preparing scientific press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing short, accurate, accessible press releases that summarize research for journalists and nonexpert readers; includes required elements (title, lead paragraph, contact info, embargo notes) and style advice. Emphasizes clarity, concision, and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall purpose and key attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release is a short summary of your research. Journalists often use press releases when deciding to write a news article on recent scientific research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The release should be clear, concise, engaging and — most importantly — accurate. Emphasize that while some science journalists are scientists, they are unlikely to be experts in every area covered, so the release must communicate the work effectively to nonexperts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility to nonexpert readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The press release should be accessible to nonexpert readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jargon and technical language; explain relevance and context. The guidance explicitly recommends writing for readers who are not specialists and structuring content so nonexperts can understand the main points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use published press releases as models
rubrics_metrics.description: Try looking through published press releases for inspiration — archived press releases can be found at news services such as EurekAlert and AlphaGalileo or on institutions’ and journals’ websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine successful examples to learn tone, length, and structure. Use those archives and institutional/journal sites as style and content benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title: short, enticing, active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep it short and enticing and use the active voice. Avoid including too much scientific detail in the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a catchy, readable title that summarizes the main news without heavy technical terms. Example contrast provided: use 'Cancer cells communicate through a new molecular messenger' rather than 'Microvesicle-derived microRNAs are important for intercellular signaling in tumorigenesis.'

rubrics_metrics.name: First paragraph: who/what/when/why; stand-alone snapshot
rubrics_metrics.description: This three–four sentence paragraph should include who (the authors), what (the main finding), when (journal and date of publication), and why (relevance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the active voice and avoid scientific jargon. The first paragraph should be a stand-alone snapshot of the research that quickly communicates the core news to a nonexpert reader or busy journalist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequent paragraphs: context and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The rest of the press release should contextualize and provide additional information about the finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the finding is exciting or unexpected and describe how the finding advances scientific knowledge, reinforces a key idea, or provides a new method. Leave out nitty-gritty experimental details in favor of broader significance. Importantly, the finding must not be overhyped or oversold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid nitty-gritty experimental detail and overhyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Nitty-gritty experimental details should be left out in favor of describing how the finding advances scientific knowledge, reinforces a key idea or provides a new method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize big-picture implications over procedural minutiae. Be careful not to overstate results — do not overhype or oversell the findings; balance enthusiasm with accuracy and appropriate caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include quotations with consent
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief quotation from a researcher involved in the work or from a colleague familiar with the importance of the finding also can be included, but be sure that they agree to be quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short, illustrative quotes that add human voice or emphasize importance, and secure explicit permission from whoever is quoted to avoid misattribution or later retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact information and access to original paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember to include contact information for the corresponding author, including their name, email, phone number and institution. Provide information for accessing the original paper, such as a URL or DOI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make it easy for journalists to follow up — complete contact details and a direct link/DOI to the publication facilitate accurate reporting and interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo information
rubrics_metrics.description: If the press release will be sent while the paper is under embargo, note the date and time that the embargo will be lifted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly mark embargo lift date/time so journalists know when they may publish stories; improper handling of embargoes can lead to broken coverage or professional issues with journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with institutional communicators and reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn how to work with your institution’s communicators and with reporters to tell the world about your research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage press offices and communications staff for help polishing messaging, arranging interviews, and distributing the release; collaboration can improve reach and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style: active voice, concise and engaging prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the active voice and keep prose concise and engaging throughout the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plain-language constructions and short sentences to maintain journalist and public interest; avoid passive constructions and excess scientific detail that reduce clarity.
